common_name: Jicarilla Apache White Corn (High-Elevation Flour-Flint Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed; this corn was selected over generations for the short, cool growing season of the Jicarilla Apache Reservation's high mountain country (roughly 6,000 feet) in northern New Mexico, so it tolerates cool nights better than lowland corn types.

directions: Jicarilla Apache White is a flour-flint corn maintained at roughly 6,000 feet elevation on the Jicarilla Apache Reservation in northern New Mexico, selected for the shorter, cooler growing season of high mountain country rather than the low desert. Ears run 6 to 8 inches long and are packed with flinty, pearl-white kernels, with an occasional pink-tinged kernel appearing in a stand. Stalks stay relatively short at 3 to 5 feet, an advantage in exposed mountain plantings, and the crop is traditionally processed into chicos, posole, and tortillas. Direct sow once the soil has warmed, since its cool-elevation origin makes it tolerant of cool nights once established but not frost-hardy as a seedling.

common_name: Gila River A'al Hu:n Corn (Akimel O'odham Flour-Flint Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost; A'al Hu:n is a low-desert flour-flint corn of the Gila River Indian Community (Akimel O'odham) in central Arizona, traditionally dry-farmed or grown with minimal irrigation through the hot low-desert season.

directions: A'al Hu:n is a traditional flour-and-flint corn of the Gila River Indian Community (Akimel O'odham) in the low desert of central Arizona, historically grown with minimal irrigation under dry-farmed or lightly irrigated conditions. Ears are relatively small but combine cream-colored flour kernels with harder, clear flint kernels on the same cob, and occasional red chinmark ears can appear from natural cross-pollination in a seed-saver's stand. It is valued for reaching maturity quickly on little water, a trait suited to the long, hot low-desert growing season. Give it full sun and warm soil, and water during establishment even though mature plants handle significant drought stress.

common_name: Pima Mottled Lima Bean (Gila River Akimel O'odham Pole Lima)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil is reliably warm; lima beans germinate poorly in cool, wet ground. This pole lima is grown by Akimel O'odham (Pima) families around St. John's in the Gila River Indian Community of Arizona and is notably drought- and heat-tolerant.

directions: Pima Mottled Lima is a pole lima bean grown by Akimel O'odham (Pima) farming families around St. John's in the Gila River Indian Community of Arizona. The pale beige seeds are patterned with black mottling in stripes, spots, and solid patches, closely resembling the related Pima Beige lima. Vigorous vines need a trellis or other support and reward it with good yields in both spring and fall low-desert plantings, tolerating heat and drought far better than lima beans bred for cooler, wetter climates. Direct sow only once the soil is reliably warm, since lima beans are slow and unreliable to germinate in cool ground.

common_name: Mountain Pima Vavuli Squash (Sierra Madre Highland Heirloom Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost danger passes; Vavuli is grown by Mountain Pima (O'ob) farmers at roughly 7,000 feet in the Sierra Madre Occidental of western Chihuahua, Mexico, a cooler highland setting than most Sonoran Desert native squash.

directions: Vavuli is a highland squash grown by Mountain Pima (O'ob) farmers in the Sierra Madre Occidental of western Chihuahua, Mexico, at elevations near 7,000 feet — considerably cooler and higher than most Sonoran Desert native cucurbits. Fruits ripen to a pale green-to-yellow skin surrounding cream-colored flesh. Because it comes from mountain rather than low-desert agriculture, it tolerates cooler nights better than many Southwestern native squash while still needing a full warm season to mature. Direct sow in warm soil after frost danger passes and give the vines ample room to sprawl.

common_name: Rarámuri Ojo de Cabra Bean (Tarahumara Sierra Madre Pole Bean)

planting.note: This Rarámuri (Tarahumara) pole bean from above 6,500 feet in Mexico's Sierra Madre is day-length sensitive and performs best sown with the summer monsoon in low-desert gardens rather than on a fixed last-frost date farther north.

directions: Ojo de Cabra, or 'Goat's Eye,' is a pole bean maintained by Rarámuri (Tarahumara) farmers at high elevation, above 6,500 feet, in Mexico's Sierra Madre. Its large seeds carry a striking pattern of dark stripes over a speckled light background inside purple-streaked pods, with occasional red, pinto, or gold-seeded beans turning up in a saved-seed population. Cooked beans are prized for a sweet, mild, creamy character that holds up well in simmered dishes like burritos and bean burgers. The variety is day-length sensitive and performs best when sown with the summer monsoon in low-desert gardens rather than on a fixed last-frost schedule farther north.

common_name: Rarámuri Vayo Bean (Tarahumara High-Elevation Pole Bean)

planting.note: Like other Rarámuri (Tarahumara) beans from the high Sierra Madre (this selection from nearly 7,800 feet), Vayo is day-length sensitive and grows and flowers best when timed to the summer monsoon rather than a strict last-frost date.

directions: Vayo is another Rarámuri (Tarahumara) pole bean from the high Sierra Madre of Mexico, selected independently from the similarly named Ojo de Cabra and distinguished by light tan seeds flecked with occasional pink and golden seed coats. The vines need sturdy trellising and, like other Rarámuri beans, are day-length sensitive, growing and setting pods best when timed to the summer monsoon rather than a strict last-frost planting date. Cooked seeds have a mild flavor and smooth, creamy texture typical of well-adapted Sierra Madre dry beans. Gardeners well north of the low desert may find it reluctant to flower and set pods before fall frost arrives.

common_name: Tohono O'odham Ha:l Squash (Sonoran Desert Edible-Seed Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost; Ha:l is a rapidly maturing, exceptionally heat-tolerant squash grown by the Tohono O'odham Nation in the low Sonoran Desert near 1,900 feet elevation, prized for both its flesh and its roasted seeds.

directions: Ha:l is a Cucurbita argyrosperma squash grown for generations by the Tohono O'odham Nation in the low Sonoran Desert near 1,900 feet elevation, valued as much for its roasted seeds as for its flesh. Mature fruit has light orange, mildly flavored, starchy flesh that stores well and can be sun-dried and resoftened by boiling later in the season; immature fruits, called ha:al mamat, are picked and cooked like zucchini. Vigorous, rapidly maturing vines are exceptionally heat tolerant and set a large fruit load even through intense desert summer heat. The blossoms are traditionally used as well, stirred into wheat flour to make a simple porridge.

common_name: Navajo Cushaw Squash (Diné Long-Necked Tail Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow in full sun after last frost; this cushaw was collected at the Navajo Fair in Shiprock, New Mexico, and is maintained at roughly 4,900 feet on the Colorado Plateau, a cooler high-desert setting than most Sonoran cushaws.

directions: Navajo Cushaw, also called Tail Squash for its long, curved neck, was collected at the Navajo Fair in Shiprock, New Mexico, and has since been maintained by seed-saving partner farmers at around 4,900 feet elevation on the Colorado Plateau. Its elongated fruit has green-and-white striped skin and a more dramatically curved neck than most other Southwestern cushaws, with cream-to-light-orange flesh inside. Like other Cucurbita argyrosperma cushaws it keeps well in storage, making it a useful winter staple for high-desert households. Direct sow after last frost in full sun and give the sprawling vines plenty of room to run.
